entries.topic: Absolute income mobility by birth cohort, 1940-1984: Chetty et al. 2017, robustness, counterfactuals, critics

claims.text: Absolute mobility (share of children with higher inflation-adjusted pre-tax family income at about age 30 than their parents at the same age) fell from 92% for the 1940 birth cohort to 50% for the 1984 cohort; 50% for the 1980 cohort; slides label the 1940 mean 91.5% and 1980 50.0%

Method: children's incomes from March CPS 1970-2014 (US-born), parents' from decennial Census/IPUMS 1940-2000; joint distribution (copula) from tax records for 1980-82 cohorts, assumed constant in baseline; 2014 dollars, CPI-U-RS deflator (CPI-U rescaled before 1977); copula bounds 84-98% (1940) and 14-88% (1984); uniform copula still gives 50% for 1980

By parent income percentile, 1940 vs 1980 cohort: 10th percentile 94% vs 70%; 50th 93% vs 45%; 90th 88% vs 33%; decline steepest in the middle class; decline especially sharp 1940-1964 cohorts, paused for late 1960s/early 1970s births

Robustness: deflator 0.8 points lower -> 93% to 59%; 2 points lower still a 26-point decline; post-tax/transfer raises levels about 3 points in all cohorts, trend unchanged; household-size adjusted 93% to 60%; at age 40, 86% (1940) to 56% (1970); sons vs fathers 95% to 41%; daughters vs fathers 43% (1940), 22% (1960), 26% (1984); adding $10,000 to 1984 incomes gives 61%

Counterfactuals for the 1980 cohort: 1940-era growth (2.5%/yr) with 1980 distribution raises absolute mobility to 62% (closing 29% of the gap); 1980 GDP with 1940 income shares raises it to 80% (closing 71%); restoring 1940 rates under today's distribution would need real GDP growth above 6% a year
State declines: Michigan about 48 points; Indiana, Illinois, Ohio about 45; Massachusetts, New York, Montana about 35; fell in all 50 states

Reeves and Guyot (Brookings 2018): largest drop between decadal cohorts was 1940 to 1950, concentrated at the top; since 1950 the greatest losses are in the middle; a child born at the 5th percentile in 1980 needs only reach about the 12th percentile to out-earn parents

Winship re-estimates summarised by Reeves and Halikias: family-size adjustment raises early-1980s cohort from 50% to 60%; PSID with PCE deflator 67%; including cash transfers 68%; Winship accepts the decline but says about two-thirds are better off

Winship (Archbridge, March 2017): roughly three in four adults, and the overwhelming majority of poor children, live better off than their parents; nearly half of bottom-fifth children stay in the bottom fifth

Strain, The American Dream Is Not Dead (2020), as reviewed: nearly three-quarters of children out-earn parents in absolute terms (household-size adjusted); 64% of children of bottom-fifth parents leave the bottom fifth and 7% reach the top fifth; reviewer VerBruggen questions household-size adjustment

Chetty et al. counterfactual slides: 'Higher growth: 1940 GDP/family growth rate (2.5%), 1980 shares'; 'More broadly shared growth: 1980 GDP/family growth rate (1.5%), 1940 shares' — growth rates are real GDP per family.

entries.topic: Relative mobility trends, geography of mobility, neighbourhood effects, MTO, social capital, race gaps, Opportunity Atlas

claims.text: Rank-rank slope (relative mobility) about 0.30 for 1971-74 (0.299), 1975-78 (0.291) and 1979-82 (0.313) cohorts; trend -0.0006 a year 1971-1993; children entering the labor market today have the same chances of moving up relative to parents as children born in the 1970s
Chetty et al. 2014: because inequality rose, 'the consequences of the birth lottery' are larger today; the gap in expected incomes between children of bottom- and top-quintile families magnified
Bottom-to-top-quintile probability 8.4% (1971 cohort) vs 9.0% (1986); college attendance gap between highest- and lowest-income children 74.5 points (1984 cohort) and 69.2 (1993)

Land of Opportunity (QJE 2014): >40 million children, 1980-82 cohorts, child income 2011-12 vs parents' 1996-2000; national rank-rank slope 0.341; bottom-to-top-quintile probability 7.5% nationally, 4.4% Charlotte, 10.8% Salt Lake City, 12.9% San Jose; absolute upward mobility 35.8 (Charlotte) to 46.2 (Salt Lake City) among 50 largest commuting zones; correlates: less segregation, less inequality, better primary schools, more social capital, more family stability; descriptive, not causal
Chetty and Hendren (QJE 2018): more than seven million families who moved; children's outcomes converge to those of the destination at about 4% per year of childhood exposure

MTO (AER 2016): children whose families used the experimental voucher to move to lower-poverty areas before age 13 earned $3,477 (31%) more a year in their mid-twenties (control mean $11,270) and attended college more; moves after 13 had, if anything, negative effects; J-PAL: 32% more likely to attend college; about 15% of voucher holders lived in neighbourhoods under 10% poverty (2017)

Nature 2022: 21 billion Facebook friendships, 72.2 million users aged 25-44; economic connectedness (share of high-SES friends among low-SES people) among strongest predictors of upward mobility; counterfactual: low-SES children in counties with EC of high-SES children would earn about 20% (19.5%) more; correlational with quasi-experimental support

Opportunity Atlas released by Census Bureau with Chetty, Hendren, Friedman 1 October 2018: over 20 million children born 1978-1983, tract-level adult earnings and incarceration; affordable 'opportunity bargains'; white men had better upward mobility than Black men almost everywhere

Atlas paper: for children of 25th-percentile parents the standard deviation of mean household income at 35 across tracts within counties is $5,000; tracts one mile away add little predictive power; observational estimates predict causal effects (MTO validation); upward mobility weakly correlated with job growth; published AER 116(1) 2026; dataset for 1984-1989 cohorts uploaded 2024

Changing Opportunity (1978-1992 cohorts): class gaps among white children widened 30%; Black children's earnings rose at all parental income levels, cutting the low-income white-Black gap 30%; explained by changes in parental employment rates within communities, mediated by social interaction

NLIHC (9 Oct 2018): the Atlas researchers identified 'opportunity bargains', affordable neighbourhoods defined as those with two-bedroom median rents under $1,500 a month that still produce good outcomes.

entries.topic: International comparison: Great Gatsby curve, IGE, OECD 2018, absolute mobility abroad, Denmark and Canada, critics

claims.text: Corak: IGE = percentage difference in child earnings per percentage difference in parental earnings; Great Gatsby curve label first used by Alan Krueger (CEA chair) 12 January 2012; Gini for disposable income about 1985 vs sons born early-mid 1960s; Finland, Norway, Denmark pass on less than a fifth; Italy, UK, US about half; US twice Canada; 'not a causal relationship' but 'too glib to dismiss'

Corak: Canada-US differences mainly at the extremes: about half of American sons of bottom-decile fathers rise no further than the third decile; more than half of sons of top-decile fathers fall no further than the 8th decile; middle similar
IGE (Corak 2012 via EPI): US 0.47, UK 0.50, Italy 0.50, France 0.41, Germany 0.32, Sweden 0.27, Australia 0.26, Canada 0.19, Finland 0.18, Norway 0.17, Denmark 0.15

OECD 2018: about four to five generations on average for a child of a bottom-10% family to reach mean income (earnings elasticity about 0.38, bottom-decile-to-mean about 1:3.5); sticky floors and sticky ceilings; in the US and Germany almost half of sons of high-earning fathers are themselves in the top quartile; report gives Nordic figures as 'about two' (executive summary) and 'at least four' (p.27)
OECD 2018 as reported: US five generations, Denmark two (PIIE); UK, Italy, Switzerland five, Denmark two, average 4.5 across 30 countries (Statista)
Kirkegaard (PIIE): Denmark's low inequality rests on high taxes and redistribution - 'no free lunch'; billionaire density similar (about 1.74 Denmark vs 1.79 US per million)

Manduca et al. 2020: absolute mobility 1960-1987 cohorts in eight countries; US and Canada near 50% for recent cohorts; Norway about 75% steady; Netherlands 0.778 (1980) to 0.686 (1984); Denmark pre-tax about 50% for 1982 (lowest) but above 65% on post-tax disposable income; differences driven mostly by marginal income distributions: US sample income grew 71% as fast as GDP vs 95% in Norway; US GDP per capita growth 1.80%/yr vs Norway 1.86%; swapping Norway's copula barely changes US absolute mobility
Manduca et al. Table A1.1.3, Canada absolute mobility on disposable income (main sample): 1977 0.575, 1978 0.580, 1979 0.579, 1980 0.575, 1982 0.565, 1983 0.568, 1984 0.571

Berman (2018): absolute mobility fell in all countries studied; decline since 1940 in percentage points: US 39.2 (growth 14.5, inequality 24.6), France 35.5, Germany 25.7, Sweden 24.9, Canada 24.1, UK 20.0, Norway 17.7, Denmark 17.2; Denmark average 78.5% vs US 62.2% for 1950-1980 cohorts

Landerso and Heckman: Denmark more mobile by income but not by education; Danish income-mobility advantage largely from redistributive taxes, transfers and wage compression; Danish child policies raise test scores without better educational outcomes

Berman decomposition of the fall in absolute mobility since 1940 (pp; growth / inequality components): Canada 24.1 (17.1/7.0), Denmark 17.2 (14.3/2.9), France 35.5 (27.9/7.7), Germany 25.7 (12.4/13.3), Norway 17.7 (12.7/5.1), Sweden 24.9 (18.0/6.9), UK 20.0 (12.5/7.5), US 39.2 (14.5/24.6); slower growth the main explanation in most countries, inequality much more important in the US.
